source.title: How to set AdamW's weight decay as you scale model and dataset size

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices. No apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally varies AdamW weight decay with dataset and model size and measures training or held-out performance. It tests weight-decay scaling, a condition in the broader claim, but does not test any listed version's specific hypothesis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on weight-decay scaling and performance across dataset and model sizes. These bear on the broader claim's explicit-regularization and model-size conditions, but the listed versions do not cover the study's particular timescale and weight-decay transfer claims. Figure-only metric values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study tests AdamW weight-decay and EMA-timescale transfer across dataset sizes and model widths, but none of V1–V8. Width sweeps do not establish generalization beyond an interpolation threshold; AdamW-only experiments do not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD; batch size is held fixed; and dropout is not varied.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors interpret AdamW weights as an EMA of recent updates and find approximately transferable optimal timescales across tested dataset sizes and widths. They recommend decreasing weight decay with dataset size and increasing it with width under muP learning-rate scaling. These empirical recommendations concern repeated-data training; exact trajectory invariance additionally requires scale-invariance and appropriately scaled initialization and optimizer settings.
record.recipe_differences: Studies AdamW weight-decay and timescale transfer across dataset and model sizes; the listed versions concern other generalization comparisons or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes depend on dataset size, model width, weight-decay parameterization, learning-rate schedule, and scale-invariance and initialization assumptions in the trajectory-invariance experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal AdamW weight decay decreases with dataset size, while the optimal EMA timescale measured in epochs is comparatively stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested repeated-data training settings with fixed batch size and learning-rate schedule, approximately preserving the EMA timescale helps transfer weight decay across dataset sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing weight decay with model width under muP learning-rate scaling makes optimal weight-decay and learning-rate settings more stable across widths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested AdamW models, scaling weight decay with width improves hyperparameter transfer by preserving the EMA timescale.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Several experiments use only one seed for LLM pre-training due to resource constraints. The paper reports averages from three seeds for image-classification tasks but does not state uncertainty intervals for the extracted results. Many relevant values appear only in figures and are not stated numerically in the text. The authors qualify trajectory invariance as requiring scale-invariant networks, learning-rate-dependent initialization, and other architectural modifications.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying outcomes beyond the figure-only performance sweeps above were extracted. Appendix figures on modified scale-invariant ResNet and ViT training trajectories and weight magnitudes were not included because they concern the paper's EMA/trajectory claims rather than the listed versions or the broader training-versus-test generalization gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error behavior beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including effects of tuning, decoupled weight decay or optimizer switching on that comparison.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes. Batch-size results discussed here come from other studies.
Dropout effects, including removing dropout and weight decay together under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Cannot_determine denotes that these rows cannot establish any listed version, not that the paper's own weight-decay findings are indeterminate. Generalization-related measurements alone do not make this a test of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Test error after widening beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with weight decay and data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or other measures that track the generalization gap.
Effects of removing memorized training examples.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance across width factors while sweeping weight decay under direct muP scaling and scaling that increases weight decay with width.

conditions.value: fixed λ versus λ = s λbase

rows.baseline: fixed λ under direct muP scaling
rows.note: The authors describe the optimal λbase and timescale as more stable when weight decay increases with width; the exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The explicitly regularized, fixed-duration width sweep does not establish zero training error or locate the interpolation threshold required by V2.

rows.subject: 8-layer GPTs
rows.operation_detail: Compared final validation loss across widths while sweeping weight decay under fixed and width-scaled weight decay parameterizations.

conditions.value: fixed λ versus λ proportional to width factor s

rows.measure: Final validation loss versus weight decay
rows.note: The authors state that optimal λbase shifts with width when λ is fixed and becomes more stable when λ increases with s.
rows.check: The width sweep does not test V2's post-interpolation claim. The value is not entirely figure-only: Figure 4 prints optimal validation losses for widths 256/512/1024. At base learning rate 3e-4 these are 3.84/3.50/3.23 under both parameterizations; at 3e-5 they are 3.94/3.60/3.36 with fixed weight decay and 3.93/3.60/3.36 with scaled weight decay.
